claim: The Drosophila midgut is maintained throughout its length by superficially similar, multipotent intestinal stem cells that generate new enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells in response to tissue requirements.
source: The Drosophila midgut is maintained throughout its length by superficially similar, multipotent intestinal stem cells that generate new enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells in response to tissue requirements.
evidence: This is a general statement about ISC function supported by the study's findings and prior literature.

claim: The midgut shows striking regional differentiation along its anterior-posterior axis with at least ten distinct subregions that differ in cell morphology, physiology and the expression of hundreds of genes.
source: We found that the midgut shows striking regional differentiation along its anterior-posterior axis. At least ten distinct subregions differ in cell morphology, physiology and the expression of hundreds of genes with likely tissue functions.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), RNAseq data showing differential gene expression (Figure 2, Supplementary file 1B), and GAL4 expression patterns (Figure 1D-G).

claim: Stem cells vary regionally in behavior and gene expression, suggesting that they contribute to midgut sub-specialization.
source: Stem cells also vary regionally in behavior and gene expression, suggesting that they contribute to midgut sub-specialization.
evidence: Supported by data showing regional differences in ISC division rates (Figure 4S), morphology (Figure 4A-C), and gene expression patterns (Figure 4E).

claim: Stem cells generate progeny located outside their own subregion at only one of six borders tested.
source: Clonal analyses showed that stem cells generate progeny located outside their own subregion at only one of six borders tested, suggesting that midgut subregions resemble cellular compartments involved in tissue development.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1 and Figure 5, showing that clones crossed only the LFC/Fe boundary but not the other five boundaries tested.

claim: Tumors generated by disrupting Notch signaling arose preferentially in three subregions and tumor cells appeared to respect regional borders.
source: Tumors generated by disrupting Notch signaling arose preferentially in three subregions and tumor cells also appeared to respect regional borders.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing tumor formation primarily in A2, P1, and P3 regions (Figure 6B-H) when Notch signaling was disrupted.

claim: Intestinal stem cells of the adult Drosophila midgut generate the two major differentiated cell types of the gut, enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells, throughout life.
source: For example, intestinal stem cells (ISCs) of the adult Drosophila midgut (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006) generate the two major differentiated cell types of the gut, enterocytes and enteroendocrine cells, throughout life.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006).

claim: ISCs with high levels of the Delta ligand specify daughters to be enterocytes via unidirectional Notch signaling.
source: ISCs with high levels of the Delta (Dl) ligand specify daughters to be enterocytes via unidirectional Notch signaling, while ISCs with low Delta levels specify enteroendocrine cell daughters (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006, 2007).

claim: ISCs with low Delta levels specify enteroendocrine cell daughters.
source: ISCs with high levels of the Delta (Dl) ligand specify daughters to be enterocytes via unidirectional Notch signaling, while ISCs with low Delta levels specify enteroendocrine cell daughters (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006, 2007).

claim: The animal's nutritional state, as sensed in part by insulin signaling, influences ISC division and whether divisions are symmetric or asymmetric.
source: The animal's nutritional state, as sensed in part by insulin signaling, influences ISC division and whether divisions are symmetric or asymmetric (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Choi et al., 2011; O'Brien et al., 2011).

claim: Dietary toxins, pathogenic bacteria, or other stressors stimulate enterocytes to release Egfr and JAK/STAT ligands that trigger nearby stem cells to multiply and produce tissue hyperplasia.
source: Dietary toxins, pathogenic bacteria, or other stressors stimulate enterocytes to release Egfr and JAK/STAT ligands that trigger nearby stem cells to multiply and produce tissue hyperplasia (reviewed in Jiang and Edgar, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review (Jiang and Edgar, 2011).

claim: ISCs that follow a generally similar program of enterocyte and enteroendocrine cell production based on Notch signaling were detected along the entire length of the midgut by clonal analysis and marker gene expression.
source: ISCs that follow a generally similar program of enterocyte and enteroendocrine cell production based on Notch signaling were detected along the entire length of the midgut by clonal analysis and marker gene expression (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).

claim: The middle midgut has an acidic pH.
source: The middle midgut has an acidic pH, and is itself tripartite in organization.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about midgut physiology.

claim: The anterior portion of the middle midgut contains specialized enterocytes known as interstitial cells.
source: The anterior portion contains specialized enterocytes known as interstitial cells (Filshie et al., 1971), interspersed with morphologically distinctive 'copper cells', which selectively fluoresce following exposure to copper ions (Poulson and Bowen, 1952; McNulty et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Filshie et al., 1971).

claim: Copper cells selectively fluoresce following exposure to copper ions.
source: The anterior portion contains specialized enterocytes known as interstitial cells (Filshie et al., 1971), interspersed with morphologically distinctive 'copper cells', which selectively fluoresce following exposure to copper ions (Poulson and Bowen, 1952; McNulty et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Poulson and Bowen, 1952; McNulty et al., 2001).

claim: The middle midgut contains a zone of 'large flat cells'.
source: There follows a zone of 'large flat cells' (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960) and an 'iron region' enriched in the iron-storage protein Ferritin (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960; Poulson and Bowen, 1952; Mehta et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960).

claim: The middle midgut contains an 'iron region' enriched in the iron-storage protein Ferritin.
source: There follows a zone of 'large flat cells' (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960) and an 'iron region' enriched in the iron-storage protein Ferritin (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960; Poulson and Bowen, 1952; Mehta et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Poulson and Waterhouse, 1960; Poulson and Bowen, 1952; Mehta et al., 2009).

claim: Copper cells depend uniquely on the homeotic gene labial during embryonic differentiation.
source: Copper cells depend uniquely on the homeotic gene labial during embryonic differentiation (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001) and function in acid production using vacuolar H+ ATPase pump proteins localized on their apical membranes (Dubreuil, 2004; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001).

claim: Copper cells function in acid production using vacuolar H+ ATPase pump proteins localized on their apical membranes.
source: Copper cells depend uniquely on the homeotic gene labial during embryonic differentiation (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001) and function in acid production using vacuolar H+ ATPase pump proteins localized on their apical membranes (Dubreuil, 2004; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Dubreuil, 2004; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).

claim: ISCs in the copper region are capable of replenishing all the major cell types, including copper, interstitial and enteroendocrine cells.
source: A recent study of ISCs in the copper region (Strand and Micchelli, 2011) found that they are capable, like posterior ISCs, of replenishing all the major cell types, including copper, interstitial and enteroendocrine cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).

claim: Copper region ISCs were reported to differ from posterior ISCs in lacking the Notch ligand Delta.
source: However, copper region ISCs were reported to differ from posterior ISCs in lacking the Notch ligand Delta, and in being normally quiescent in the absence of stress (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Strand and Micchelli, 2011), though the current study contradicts this finding.

claim: Copper region ISCs were reported to be normally quiescent in the absence of stress.
source: However, copper region ISCs were reported to differ from posterior ISCs in lacking the Notch ligand Delta, and in being normally quiescent in the absence of stress (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Strand and Micchelli, 2011), though the current study shows they divide regularly every 4-5 days.

claim: Some digestive enzymes show restricted spatial localization in midguts from a variety of insects.
source: The possible existence of regional variation is further suggested by the restricted spatial localization of some digestive enzymes in midguts from a variety of insects (reviewed by Terra and Ferreira, 1994) and from Drosophila larvae.
evidence: Supported by citation to a review (Terra and Ferreira, 1994).

claim: The lipase Magro may be trafficked into the midgut from the proventriculus via the peritrophic matrix.
source: Some enzymes, such as the lipase Magro (Sieber and Thummel, 2012), may be trafficked into the midgut from the proventriculus via the peritrophic matrix (King, 1988).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Sieber and Thummel, 2012; King, 1988).

claim: α-amylase is expressed primarily in the anterior and posterior midgut regions.
source: Others such as, α-amylase, which is expressed primarily in the anterior and posterior midgut regions (Thompson et al., 1992) probably indicate true regional differences in enterocyte expression.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Thompson et al., 1992).

claim: Unique neuropeptides are secreted by enteroendocrine cells located in specific gut regions.
source: Some of the strongest evidence for further regionalization comes from studies showing that unique neuropeptides are secreted by enteroendocrine cells located in specific gut regions (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Veenstra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Veenstra et al., 2008).

claim: Only fertilized adult females 4–14 days of age were employed to avoid the final steps of gut maturation that take place in young adults and age-induced decline.
source: Only, fertilized adult females 4–14 days of age were employed to avoid the final steps of gut maturation that take place in young adults (Takashima et al., 2013a), as well as age-induced decline (O'Brian et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale, supported by citations (Takashima et al., 2013a; O'Brian et al., 2011).

claim: Under controlled conditions, the cellular structure of the midgut was stable and reproducible as assessed by cell counts along its length.
source: Under these conditions, the cellular structure of the midgut was stable and reproducible as assessed by cell counts along its length (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C showing reproducible cell counts.

claim: EM analyses of longitudinally sectioned midguts revealed many more reproducible regional differences in enterocyte structure than those described previously in the middle midgut.
source: EM analyses of longitudinally sectioned midguts revealed many more reproducible regional differences in enterocyte structure than those described previously in the middle midgut, including differences in cell type, cell size, membrane invaginations, microvillar length, and the presence of ferritin particles, glycogen or lipid droplets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Differences in enterocyte structure were summarized in scale drawings that define 10 distinct zones along the a/p axis.
source: Differences were summarized in scale drawings that define 10 distinct zones along the a/p axis (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by the schematic drawing in Figure 1A.

claim: Ferritin-GFP selectively stained the Fe region.
source: Ferritin-GFP selectively stained the Fe region, while Nile red, which stains lipid droplets, marked the A2, P1 and P3 zones (Figure 1B), the same regions showing enterocytes with high lipid content in EM images.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy data in Figure 1B.

claim: Nile red marked the A2, P1 and P3 zones, the same regions showing enterocytes with high lipid content in EM images.
source: Ferritin-GFP selectively stained the Fe region, while Nile red, which stains lipid droplets, marked the A2, P1 and P3 zones (Figure 1B), the same regions showing enterocytes with high lipid content in EM images.
evidence: Supported by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1B) and EM data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The number of enterocyte cell diameters along the a/p axis within each section was highly reproducible.
source: The number of enterocyte cell diameters along the a/p axis within each section was recorded for multiple guts and these proved to be highly reproducible (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data with error bars shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The correspondence of gene expression boundaries in endodermal cells with the morphological junctions of the 10 subregions was striking.
source: The correspondence of gene expression boundaries in endodermal cells with the morphological junctions of the 10 subregions was striking (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by the summary of GAL4 expression boundaries shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Gene expression boundaries in gut muscle were mostly offset from the endodermal region boundaries.
source: In contrast, gene expression boundaries in gut muscle were mostly offset from these boundaries (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by the summary of muscle GAL4 expression boundaries shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RNA samples from 30 separate preparations derived from 10 different single or grouped regions were analyzed by RNAseq using paired-end reads of 100 × 100 nucleotides and a depth of 30–110 million reads.
source: RNA samples from 30 separate preparations derived from 10 different single or grouped regions (Figure 2A) were analyzed by RNAseq using paired-end reads of 100 × 100 nucleotides and a depth of 30–110 million reads (Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This describes the RNAseq methodology used in the study.

claim: The expression of Npf and Ast-A mRNAs was observed within the middle and posterior regions.
source: For example, the expression of the neuropeptides Npf and Ast-A is patterned within the midgut (Veenstra et al., 2008) and we observed expression of the corresponding mRNAs within the middle and posterior regions, as predicted, along with patterned expression of many other previously unlocalized neuropeptide mRNAs (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2B,D and citation to prior work (Veenstra et al., 2008).

claim: The labial gene encodes a homeobox transcription factor that is only expressed in the copper cell region.
source: The labial (lab) gene encodes a homeobox transcription factor that is only expressed in the copper cell region, where it is required for copper cell differentiation (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001; Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001; Strand and Micchelli, 2011).

claim: Labial is required for copper cell differentiation.
source: The labial (lab) gene encodes a homeobox transcription factor that is only expressed in the copper cell region, where it is required for copper cell differentiation (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001; Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Panganiban et al., 1990; Hoppler and Bienz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001; Strand and Micchelli, 2011).

claim: Lab fpkm was 40–100 times higher in isolated Cu region RNA than in any other adult midgut region.
source: Revealingly, lab fpkm was 40–100 times higher in isolated Cu region RNA than in any other adult midgut region (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All seven of the midgut segments that were isolated showed highly specific gene expression.
source: All seven of the midgut segments we were able to isolate showed highly specific gene expression.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing region-specific expression of multiple genes (Figure 2D).

claim: CG10725 was enriched in A1, along with many other genes involved in chitin metabolism, where it likely encodes a component of the peritrophic membrane.
source: CG10725 was enriched in A1 (Figure 2D), along with many other genes involved in chitin metabolism, where it likely encodes a component of the peritrophic membrane.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data (Figure 2D) and inference about function based on co-expression with chitin metabolism genes.

claim: Beta-galactosidase (Gal) mRNA was selectively found in the A2-A3 sample.
source: Although their levels of spatial specificity were not previously known, Beta-galactosidase (Gal) mRNA was selectively found in the A2-A3 sample, the ZIP1 iron transporter mRNA in the Fe region, and the CG3106 acyl transferase mRNA in P1.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The ZIP1 iron transporter mRNA was found in the Fe region.
source: Although their levels of spatial specificity were not previously known, Beta-galactosidase (Gal) mRNA was selectively found in the A2-A3 sample, the ZIP1 iron transporter mRNA in the Fe region, and the CG3106 acyl transferase mRNA in P1.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The CG3106 acyl transferase mRNA was found in P1.
source: Although their levels of spatial specificity were not previously known, Beta-galactosidase (Gal) mRNA was selectively found in the A2-A3 sample, the ZIP1 iron transporter mRNA in the Fe region, and the CG3106 acyl transferase mRNA in P1.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The high specificity of gene expression proves that cross-contamination was minimal and that gene expression boundaries correspond to the regional boundaries used in tissue isolation.
source: This high specificity proves that cross-contamination was minimal and that gene expression boundaries correspond to the regional boundaries used in tissue isolation, while the correspondence of the RNAseq data to previous studies of gene expression validates the reliability of this large new body of information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high regional specificity of gene expression observed in the RNAseq data.

claim: PGRPs are membrane proteins that mediate interactions between the midgut and the microbiome that are essential for normal digestion.
source: For example, PGRPs are membrane proteins that mediate interactions between the midgut and the microbiome that are essential for normal digestion (Cash et al., 2006; Ryu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Cash et al., 2006; Ryu et al., 2008).

claim: PGRP-SC1b and PGRP-SC2 expression was highly enriched in the LFC and Fe regions, respectively, along with their regulator, caudal.
source: PGRP-SC1b and PGRP-SC2 expression was found to be highly enriched in the LFC and Fe regions, respectively, along with their regulator, caudal (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The localized expression of PGRP family members suggests that the microbiome interacts with enterocytes in a highly organized way and that some bacterial species may be localized to specific regions of the gut lumen by the selective expression of host factors.
source: The localized expression of these and other PGRP family members (Figure 2C) suggest that the microbiome interacts with enterocytes in a highly organized way and that some bacterial species may be localized to specific regions of the gut lumen by the selective expression of host factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regional expression patterns of PGRP genes.

claim: Each isolated subregion expressed 50–150 genes 10 times higher than in any other selected subregion of the midgut.
source: Each isolated subregion expressed 50–150 genes 10 times higher than in any other selected subregion of the midgut (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: The anterior, middle and posterior zones each expressed 259–474 genes at least five times more highly than in the other two zones.
source: The anterior, middle and posterior zones each expressed 259–474 genes at least five times more highly than in the other two zones, and differentially expressed mRNAs represented some of the most highly expressed genes in each region (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data analysis presented in Supplementary file 1B.

claim: Many regionally expressed midgut genes reside in genomic clusters like highly expressed genes in many other differentiated cells.
source: Interestingly, many regionally expressed midgut genes reside in genomic clusters like highly expressed genes in many other differentiated cells (Spellman and Rubin, 2002).
evidence: Supported by observation from the RNAseq data and citation to prior work (Spellman and Rubin, 2002).

claim: Regionally expressed genes include trypsins, lysozymes, serine proteases, alpha-glucosidases, lipases and Jonah genes.
source: These included trypsins, lysozymes, serine proteases, alpha-glucosidases, lipases and Jonah genes (Akam and Carlson, 1985).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and citation to prior work (Akam and Carlson, 1985).

claim: In A1, where enterocytes are more squamous and shorter than in other regions, the stem cells were flatter than the upward-directed triangular shape seen in all other regions.
source: In A1, where enterocytes are more squamous and shorter than in other regions, the stem cells were flatter than the upward-directed triangular shape seen in all other regions (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: In the most lipid-rich region, P1, ISCs often contained many lipid droplets and reported lipid synthesis using the SREBP-GAL4 reporter line.
source: Additionally, in the most lipid-rich region, P1, ISCs often contained many lipid droplets and reported lipid synthesis using the SREBP-GAL4 reporter line (Matthews et al., 2009) (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy (Figure 4C) and reporter line expression data, with citation (Matthews et al., 2009).

claim: Two lines, R42G03 (Pdp1) and R44E05 (Stat92E), were differentially expressed in ISCs.
source: Two lines uncovered in the screen, R42G03 (Pdp1) and R44E05 (Stat92E), were differentially expressed in ISCs (Figure 4E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the boundaries of expression coincided with regional boundaries.
evidence: Supported by GAL4 expression pattern data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Using improved staining conditions, Dl+ cells with the characteristics of ISCs were detected in all 10 regions, including the Cu region.
source: Using improved staining conditions ('Materials and methods'), we detected Dl+ cells with the characteristics of ISCs in all 10 regions (Figure 4F–O), including the Cu region (Figure 4I), where Delta expression in ISCs was previously reported to be absent (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F-O, contradicting a prior report (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).

claim: ISCs divided at different rates in different regions based on clonal marking.
source: However, ISCs divided at different rates in different regions based on clonal marking (Figure 4S).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 4S.

claim: The most rapidly dividing ISCs are found in P1-P3, which divide about once per day.
source: The most rapidly dividing ISCs are found in P1-P3, which divide about once per day, while ISC division is slightly less frequent in the anterior midgut, and much slower in the middle region.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 4S.

claim: Cu region ISCs divided regularly every 4–5 days.
source: However, in contrast to a previous report (Strand and Micchelli, 2011), Cu region ISCs were not entirely quiescent but divided regularly every 4–5 days.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 4S, contradicting a prior report (Strand and Micchelli, 2011).

claim: ISCs in different regions maintain differing numbers of enteroendocrine cells and enterocytes.
source: ISCs in different regions maintain differing numbers of enteroendocrine cells and enterocytes (Figure 4R).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4R.

claim: In P1 (and to a lesser extent in P3 and A2), the enteroblast and even the youngest EC continued to stain for Dl.
source: Interestingly, in P1 (and to a lesser extent in P3 and A2), the enteroblast and even the youngest EC continued to stain for Dl (Figure 4L′).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4L′.

claim: The persistent Delta in enteroblasts in the P1 region likely leads to persistent Notch activation during early enterocyte differentiation.
source: Although ISCs generated the same cells as elsewhere in the midgut, the persistent Delta in enteroblasts in the P1 region likely leads to persistent Notch activation during early enterocyte differentiation; the Notch activity reporter GbeSu(H)-lacZ was expressed in young ECs in P1 and P3, but not in other regions (Figure 4Q vs 4P).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of persistent Delta expression and Notch reporter activity shown in Figure 4P-Q.

claim: The Notch activity reporter GbeSu(H)-lacZ was expressed in young ECs in P1 and P3, but not in other regions.
source: Although ISCs generated the same cells as elsewhere in the midgut, the persistent Delta in enteroblasts in the P1 region likely leads to persistent Notch activation during early enterocyte differentiation; the Notch activity reporter GbeSu(H)-lacZ was expressed in young ECs in P1 and P3, but not in other regions (Figure 4Q vs 4P).
evidence: Supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 4P-Q.

claim: Clones in the midgut sometimes run for a considerable distance perpendicular to the a/p axis, but rarely if ever parallel to the axis.
source: We noticed that clones in the midgut sometimes run for a considerable distance perpendicular to the a/p axis (Figure 5A), but rarely if ever parallel to the axis.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Among more than 3000 sparse clones generated throughout the midgut, rare 'boundary clones' were identified that contained a single stem cell, at least four total cells and that contacted a marked boundary from one side or the other.
source: Among more than 3000 sparse clones generated throughout the midgut, we identified rare 'boundary clones' that contained a single stem cell, at least four total cells and that contacted a marked boundary from one side or the other.
evidence: This describes the methodology and criteria for identifying boundary clones in the clonal analysis.

claim: 49 unambiguous boundary clones contacting six different regional boundaries were characterized.
source: However, we characterized 49 unambiguous boundary clones contacting six different regional boundaries (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Boundary clones that resulted from stem cell labeling within A1 or A2 contacted the border zone but never included cells from the opposite side.
source: Boundary clones that resulted from stem cell labeling within A1 (Figure 5D,D′) or A2 (Figure 5E,E′) contacted the border zone defined by R45D10::UAS-GFP expression, but never included cells from the opposite side.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 5D-E and Table 1.

claim: Clones failed to differentiate heterologously across four other studied boundaries, including Fe/P1 and P1/P2.
source: Similarly, clones failed to differentiate heterologously across four other studied boundaries (Table 1), including Fe/P1 (Figure 5H,I) and P1/P2 (Figure 5J,K).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 5H-K and Table 1.

claim: Clones readily crossed the boundary between LFC and Fe, and differentiated or transformed into cells characteristic of the opposite side.
source: Clones readily crossed one boundary, between LFC and Fe, and differentiated or transformed into cells characteristic of the opposite side.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 5F-G and Table 1.

claim: 15 of 17 clones crossed the LFC/Fe boundary, and did so readily from either direction.
source: 15 of 17 clones crossed the boundary, and did so readily from either direction (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 5F-G and Table 1.

claim: 88% of boundary clones on the LFC/Fe boundary crossed and generated cells on the other side.
source: For example, 88% of boundary clones on the LFC/Fe boundary crossed and generated cells on the other side (N = 17).
evidence: Calculated from the clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border.
source: In comparison, 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border (N = 6), 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border (N = 3), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border (N = 4), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border (N = 7), and 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border (N = 12).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border.
source: In comparison, 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border (N = 6), 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border (N = 3), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border (N = 4), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border (N = 7), and 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border (N = 12).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border.
source: In comparison, 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border (N = 6), 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border (N = 3), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border (N = 4), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border (N = 7), and 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border (N = 12).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border.
source: In comparison, 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border (N = 6), 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border (N = 3), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border (N = 4), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border (N = 7), and 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border (N = 12).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border.
source: In comparison, 0% of boundary clones crossed the A1/A2 border (N = 6), 0% of boundary clones crossed the A3/Cu border (N = 3), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Cu/LFC border (N = 4), 0% of boundary clones crossed the Fe/P1 border (N = 7), and 0% of boundary clones crossed the P1/P2 border (N = 12).
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: The differences in boundary crossing behavior between LFC/Fe and other boundaries are statistically significant.
source: These differences are all statistically significant, since the probability that even three boundary clones would fail to cross a junction equivalent to the LFC/Fe boundary is only (1–0.88)3 = 0.0017.
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the clonal data from Table 1.

claim: In boundary clones at the LFC/Fe border, there were 0.63 crossing cells for every boundary cell.
source: In boundary clones at the LFC/Fe border, there were 0.63 crossing cells for every boundary cell (N = 115).
evidence: Calculated from the clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: Disrupting Notch signaling in ISCs leads to enteroendocrine tumor formation.
source: Disrupting Notch signaling in ISCs leads to enteroendocrine tumor formation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of Notch signaling in ISCs.

claim: Tumorous cells arose and proliferated much more extensively in some midgut subregions than in others.
source: Surprisingly, tumorous cells arose and proliferated much more extensively in some midgut subregions than in others (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The P1 region consistently had the largest tumors and earliest onset.
source: The P1 region consistently had the largest tumors and earliest onset, although tumors also arose rapidly in P3 and the posterior part of A2.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: Tumors also arose rapidly in P3 and the posterior part of A2.
source: The P1 region consistently had the largest tumors and earliest onset, although tumors also arose rapidly in P3 and the posterior part of A2.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Tumors were never observed within A1, even after long periods of exposure to Notch inhibition.
source: In contrast, we never observed tumors within A1, even after long periods of exposure to these agents.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations from Notch inhibition experiments.

claim: As the tumor cells expanded they appeared to respect the cellular boundaries with adjacent midgut regions.
source: As the tumor cells expanded they appeared to respect the cellular boundaries with adjacent midgut regions.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6D-H.

claim: The anterior border of P1 tumor cells corresponded closely with the Fe/P1 boundary based on counts of cell diameters from the Cu region.
source: For example, the anterior border of P1 tumor cells corresponded closely with the Fe/P1 boundary based on counts of cell diameters from the Cu region (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The posterior boundary of P1 tumor expansion mapped near or at the P1/P2 border.
source: The posterior boundary of P1 tumor expansion mapped near or at the P1/P2 border (Figure 6F), while the anterior and posterior boundaries of P3 tumors also corresponded with their normal junctions with P2 (Figure 6G) and P3/P4 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The anterior and posterior boundaries of P3 tumors corresponded with their normal junctions with P2 and P3/P4.
source: The posterior boundary of P1 tumor expansion mapped near or at the P1/P2 border (Figure 6F), while the anterior and posterior boundaries of P3 tumors also corresponded with their normal junctions with P2 (Figure 6G) and P3/P4 (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: The same regional specificity of tumor formation was observed when Notch signaling was inhibited using N[RNAi], treatment with the Notch inhibitor DAPT, or by expressing a Notch-dominative negative allele NDN.
source: The same regional specificity was observed when Notch signaling was inhibited using N[RNAi], treatment with the Notch inhibitor DAPT, or by expressing a Notch-dominative negative allele NDN.
evidence: This indicates that the regional tumor specificity is robust across different methods of Notch inhibition.

claim: Regional epigenetic differences have a large effect on the development of midgut enteroendocrine tumors.
source: These results indicate that regional epigenetic differences have a large effect on the development of midgut enteroendocrine tumors and that regional boundaries restrict tumor cell movement into adjacent tissue compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regional differences in tumor formation and boundary respect.

claim: Regional boundaries restrict tumor cell movement into adjacent tissue compartments.
source: These results indicate that regional epigenetic differences have a large effect on the development of midgut enteroendocrine tumors and that regional boundaries restrict tumor cell movement into adjacent tissue compartments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that tumor cells respect regional boundaries.

claim: Regionalization likely supports the complex metabolic tasks carried out by the midgut.
source: Regionalization likely supports the complex metabolic tasks carried out by the midgut.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regional differences in gene expression and cell morphology.

claim: Ingested food goes through multiple intermediate stages during digestion and these steps may be most efficient if carried out in a controlled sequence.
source: Ingested food goes through multiple intermediate stages during digestion and these steps may be most efficient if carried out in a controlled sequence (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regional specialization and gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Some digestive steps are associated with an array of bacterial species that constitute the normal intestinal microbiome.
source: Some of these steps are associated with an array of bacterial species that constitute the normal intestinal microbiome (Ryu et al., 2008; Shin et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ryu et al., 2008; Shin et al., 2011).

claim: After this work was submitted for publication, Buchon et al. (2013) also described midgut regionalization with five major midgut divisions (R1–R5), 13 total subregions, and 2 microregions.
source: After this work was submitted for publication, Buchon et al. (2013) also described midgut regionalization; they classified five major midgut divisions (R1–R5), 13 total subregions (e.g., R1a and R1b), and 2 microregions (BR2–3, BR3–4).
evidence: This references a concurrent study by Buchon et al. (2013) that independently described midgut regionalization.

claim: There is a close correspondence between the regions defined in this study and those defined by Buchon et al. (2013).
source: Converting our counts of cell number within the 10 regions (Figure 1C) to the fractional length coordinates used by Buchon et al. (2013) suggests a close correspondence between the studies: A1 = R1a + R1b; A2 = R2a + R2b; A3 = R2c; Cu = R3a + R3b; LFC = R3c; Fe = BR3–R4, P1 = R4a + R4b; P2 = R4c; P3 = R5a; P4 = R5b.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's regions and those defined by Buchon et al. (2013).

claim: The striking regionalization of structure and gene expression within the midgut is maintained at least in part by regional differences between their resident stem cells.
source: Our results argue strongly that the striking regionalization of structure and gene expression within the midgut is maintained at least in part by regional differences between their resident stem cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clonal analysis data showing that stem cells do not cross most regional boundaries.

claim: In the midgut subregions surrounding five different boundaries, not a single stem cell was detected that produced differentiated cells on the opposite side of the boundary.
source: In the midgut subregions surrounding five different boundaries, we did not detect a single stem cell that produced differentiated cells on the opposite side of the boundary, that is from a region different from the one in which it resided.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data presented in Table 1 and Figure 5.

claim: All the 'non-crossing' clones contacted the regional boundary, and in 78% the founder stem cell was located on or within one cell of the boundary.
source: All the 'non-crossing' clones contacted the regional boundary, and in 78% the founder stem cell was located on or within one cell of the boundary, such that progeny cells could have reached the adjacent region prior to differentiation.
evidence: Calculated from the clonal analysis data presented in Table 1.

claim: Boundary clones with the same general properties almost always crossed the LFC/Fe boundary, showing that 'non-crossing' behavior would not occur by chance.
source: In contrast, boundary clones with the same general properties almost always crossed the LFC/Fe boundary, showing that 'non-crossing' behavior would not occur by chance.
evidence: Supported by clonal analysis data showing 88% of LFC/Fe boundary clones crossed (Table 1).

claim: Clones frequently pushed into adjacent regions at the boundary, but retained their autonomous identity based on marker expression.
source: Consistent with the existence of epigenetic differences in stem cells that limit trans-regional differentiation, clones frequently pushed into adjacent regions at the boundary, but retained their autonomous identity based on marker expression.
evidence: This is an observation from the clonal analysis experiments.

claim: Mechanical and/or adhesive forces may also contribute to maintaining some regional boundaries.
source: Mechanical and/or adhesive forces may also contribute to maintaining some regional boundaries.
evidence: This is speculation about additional mechanisms that might maintain boundaries.

claim: The tendency of tumor cells to respect regional boundaries suggests that cell–cell interactions at boundaries are likely to be important as well as stem cell programming.
source: Indeed, the tendency of tumor cells to respect regional boundaries suggests that cell–cell interactions at boundaries are likely to be important as well as stem cell programming.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that tumor cells respect regional boundaries.

claim: The behavior of ISC clones at regional boundaries is reminiscent of the behavior of clones in developing imaginal discs at 'compartment' boundaries.
source: The behavior of ISC clones at regional boundaries is reminiscent of the behavior of clones in developing imaginal discs at 'compartment' boundaries (reviewed in Dahmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to known developmental biology phenomena, supported by citation (Dahmann et al., 2011).

claim: In the developing Drosophila embryo and imaginal discs, the engrailed gene and hedgehog signaling play important roles in defining posterior compartments.
source: In the developing Drosophila embryo and imaginal discs, the engrailed gene and hedgehog signaling play important roles in defining posterior compartments (Dahmann and Basler, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Dahmann and Basler, 2000).

claim: Engrailed or the closely related gene invected were not detected in any midgut region.
source: We did not detect expression of engrailed or the closely related gene invected in any midgut region, and expression of hedgehog pathway components was similar on both sides of non-crossing boundaries such as Fe/P1.
evidence: Based on analysis of the RNAseq data.

claim: Expression of hedgehog pathway components was similar on both sides of non-crossing boundaries such as Fe/P1.
source: We did not detect expression of engrailed or the closely related gene invected in any midgut region, and expression of hedgehog pathway components was similar on both sides of non-crossing boundaries such as Fe/P1.
evidence: Based on analysis of the RNAseq data.

claim: Dorsal ventral compartments in the developing wing are mediated by apterous and by Notch signaling.
source: Dorsal ventral compartments in the developing wing are mediated by apterous and by Notch signaling (Milan and Cohen, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Milan and Cohen, 2003).

claim: Apterous was expressed only at very low levels throughout all regions.
source: Apterous was expressed only at very low levels throughout all regions and Serrate was found at significant levels only in posterior regions 2–4 where the gene is dispensable for cell differentiation (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Based on analysis of the RNAseq data and citation to prior work (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).

claim: Serrate was found at significant levels only in posterior regions 2–4 where the gene is dispensable for cell differentiation.
source: Apterous was expressed only at very low levels throughout all regions and Serrate was found at significant levels only in posterior regions 2–4 where the gene is dispensable for cell differentiation (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Based on analysis of the RNAseq data and citation to prior work (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).

claim: In the developing vertebrate brain, Hox genes are important in specifying developmental compartments.
source: In the developing vertebrate brain, Hox genes are important in specifying developmental compartments (Kiecker and Lumsden, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Kiecker and Lumsden, 2005).

claim: Hox genes are only expressed at very low levels in endodermal cells during embryogenesis.
source: However, Hox genes are only expressed at very low levels in endodermal cells during embryogenesis (Hoppler and Beinz, 1994) and these genes were very weakly expressed in our RNAseq studies, perhaps due to expression in non-endodermal cells within these samples.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data and citation to prior work (Hoppler and Beinz, 1994).

claim: The genetic basis for adult midgut compartmentalization probably differs from previously studied examples of tissue regionalization.
source: Consequently, the genetic basis for adult midgut compartmentalization probably differs from previously studied examples of tissue regionalization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of expression of known compartment-defining genes in the midgut.

claim: The homeotic transcription factor labial (lab) is an outstanding candidate for a regional regulatory factor.
source: The homeotic transcription factor labial (lab) is an outstanding candidate for a regional regulatory factor.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known role of labial in copper cell specification.

claim: In the embryonic and larval gut, lab is required for Cu cell specification, differentiation and maintenance.
source: In the embryonic and larval gut, lab is required for Cu cell specification, differentiation and maintenance (Hoppler and Beinz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hoppler and Beinz, 1994; Dubreuil et al., 2001).

claim: Lab is expressed in copper cells, but not elsewhere in the larval midgut.
source: The gene is expressed in copper cells, but not elsewhere in the larval midgut, and we observed similar specificity of lab expression in the adult.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data showing lab expression only in the Cu region.

claim: When lab is mis-expressed during embryonic development in other midgut regions, the copper region can expand.
source: When lab is mis-expressed during embryonic development in other midgut regions, the copper region can expand (Hoppler and Bienz, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Hoppler and Bienz, 1994).

claim: Endodermal cell identity along the a/p axis may be determined by signals from adjacent mesoderm during embryogenesis, and then fixed by the induction of secondary factors such as lab.
source: Endodermal cell identity along the a/p axis may be determined by signals from adjacent mesoderm during embryogenesis (Bilder and Scott, 1998), and then fixed by the induction of secondary factors such as lab.
evidence: This is speculation based on prior work (Bilder and Scott, 1998) about how regional identity might be established.

claim: Gene expression within the midgut muscles might play a similar role in the adult midgut.
source: Gene expression within the midgut muscles might play a similar role in the adult midgut, however, expression boundaries of muscle genes were frequently offset with respect to endodermal regions (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is speculation, but noted that muscle gene boundaries are offset from endodermal boundaries (Figure 1E).

claim: The homeotic gene defective proventriculus (dve) functions in copper cells.
source: For example, one potential candidate, the homeotic gene defective proventriculus (dve), functions in copper cells (Nakagawa et al., 2011) and its expression was observed to fall sixfold between Fe and P1.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Nakagawa et al., 2011) and RNAseq data.

claim: Dve expression was observed to fall sixfold between Fe and P1.
source: For example, one potential candidate, the homeotic gene defective proventriculus (dve), functions in copper cells (Nakagawa et al., 2011) and its expression was observed to fall sixfold between Fe and P1.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data analysis.

claim: The larval gut has a middle acidic region containing copper cells and an iron region like the adult tissue.
source: The larval gut has a middle acidic region containing copper cells and an iron region like the adult tissue (Poulson and Bowen, 1952), and EM studies show additional morphological differences (Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Poulson and Bowen, 1952; Shanbhag and Tripathi, 2009).

claim: The larval midgut contains nests of diploid intestinal precursors that proliferate following pupariation to build the adult gut and establish its ISCs.
source: The larval midgut contains nests of diploid intestinal precursors that proliferate following pupariation to build the adult gut and establish its ISCs (Jiang and Edgar, 2009; Mathur et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Jiang and Edgar, 2009; Mathur et al., 2010).

claim: Cells do cross boundaries between the hindgut and midgut during pupal gut development.
source: However, cells do cross boundaries between the hindgut and midgut during pupal gut development (Takashima et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Takashima et al., 2013b).

claim: Identical regionalization within larval and adult guts might be disadvantageous to species with very different larval and adult diets.
source: Identical regionalization within larval and adult guts might be disadvantageous to species with very different larval and adult diets, hence many adult midgut regions are likely to be established de novo or to be re-specified during pupal development.
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary and developmental logic of midgut regionalization.

claim: Many adult midgut regions are likely to be established de novo or to be re-specified during pupal development.
source: Identical regionalization within larval and adult guts might be disadvantageous to species with very different larval and adult diets, hence many adult midgut regions are likely to be established de novo or to be re-specified during pupal development.
evidence: This is speculation about how adult midgut regions are established.

claim: Similar stem cells expressing Lgr5 exist along the mammalian gut despite the fact that enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells and bacterial symbionts differ regionally.
source: Lineage labeling shows that similar stem cells expressing Lgr5 exist along the mammalian gut (Barker et al., 2007) despite the fact that enterocytes, enteroendocrine cells and bacterial symbionts differ regionally (Rindi et al., 2004; Bradley et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Barker et al., 2007; Rindi et al., 2004; Bradley et al., 2011).

claim: Iron absorption in mammals takes place primarily in the duodenum, a specialized subregion of the small intestine located just downstream from the acidic stomach.
source: For example, iron absorption in mammals takes place primarily in the duodenum (Fuqua et al., 2012), a specialized subregion of the small intestine located just downstream from the acidic stomach.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Fuqua et al., 2012).

claim: The position of the mammalian duodenum is similar to the position of the midgut iron region just downstream from the acid-producing parietal cells of the Cu and LFC regions.
source: This is similar to the position of the midgut iron region just downstream from the acid-producing parietal cells of the Cu and LFC regions.
evidence: This is a comparison between mammalian and Drosophila gut organization.

claim: The antibacterial lectin RegIIIγ is expressed most prominently in the distal region of the small intestine.
source: The antibacterial lectin RegIIIγ, which like Drosophila PGRPs recognizes bacterial peptidoglycans, is expressed most prominently in the distal region of the small intestine (Cash et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Cash et al., 2006).

claim: The human large intestine is much more prone to cancer than the small intestine.
source: The human large intestine is much more prone to cancer than the small intestine.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: Regional differences in the properties of apparently similar stem cells and tissue cells contribute to differences in cancer susceptibility.
source: Our studies suggest that regional differences in the properties of apparently similar stem cells and tissue cells contribute to such differences.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed regional differences in tumor formation in the Drosophila midgut.

claim: The midgut zones most favorable for the expansion of Notch-deficient cells showed pre-existing differences in Notch signaling within the early enterocyte lineage.
source: The midgut zones most favorable for the expansion of Notch-deficient cells showed pre-existing differences in Notch signaling within the early enterocyte lineage.
evidence: Supported by data showing persistent Delta expression and Notch reporter activity in P1 and P3 (Figure 4P-Q).

claim: Delta expression did not decrease shortly after ISC division in tumor-prone regions, and Notch signaling persisted throughout enterocyte development.
source: Delta expression did not decrease shortly after ISC division, as in other regions, and Notch signaling persisted throughout enterocyte development (Figure 4Q).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and reporter data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: Tumor-prone regions with persistent Notch signaling were also enriched in lipid droplets.
source: Curiously, same tumor-prone regions with persistent Notch signaling also were enriched in lipid droplets (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by EM and Nile red staining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Regional differences in the microbiome, as suggested by domain-specific expression of PGRP proteins, may also influence the occurrence of cancer.
source: Additionally, regional differences in the microbiome, as suggested by our observation of domain-specific expression of PGRP proteins, may also influence the occurrence of cancer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed regional expression of PGRP genes and known roles of the microbiome in cancer.

claim: Gastric bacteria such as Helicobacter pylori contribute to stomach cancer.
source: Gastric bacteria such as Helicobacter pylori contribute to stomach cancer (Uemura et al., 2001), while colonic Bacteroides fragilis likely promote gut cell DNA damage and colon cancer (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Uemura et al., 2001).

claim: Colonic Bacteroides fragilis likely promote gut cell DNA damage and colon cancer.
source: Gastric bacteria such as Helicobacter pylori contribute to stomach cancer (Uemura et al., 2001), while colonic Bacteroides fragilis likely promote gut cell DNA damage and colon cancer (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Wu et al., 2009).

claim: Regional tissue differences likely also affect rates of tumor progression and metastasis.
source: Regional tissue differences likely also affect rates of tumor progression and metastasis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed regional differences in tumor formation.
